lines: The fraud model's own average score time sits comfortably inside the checkout's budget, no problem there at all.
The checkout's actual ninety-ninth percentile, though, blows straight past the timeout.
The fallback on timeout here is simply "approve" — and the fraud loss this model was bought to prevent concentrates in exactly those payments.
The average was genuinely never the number that mattered here.
So where did that percentile actually go, and what should the fallback have been instead?
answer: The average score time was already comfortable, so a faster model would be attacking entirely the wrong number.
The real problem lives in one hop's own tail, and the fallback itself deserves a recorded decision, never just a default.

lines: An event arrives, and streaming features update incrementally from it.
The request path then looks those exact features up, a model scores them, and a decision returns.
A boundary separates the stream job's own eventually-consistent features from the request path's read of whatever the store happens to hold right now.
A hundred-millisecond budget splits across hops — network in, feature lookup, model inference, rules, network out.
Each one gets measured at its own ninety-ninth percentile, never its average.
One single hop's own tail overflows its share.
A budget built from averages hides exactly the hop that genuinely blows the deadline, which is why it has to be built at that percentile instead, hop by hop.
Adding up every single hop's own ninety-ninth percentile gives you a ceiling the design can plan against, nothing more.
The chain's own actually measured percentile sits below that ceiling, because the hops' latencies simply aren't independent of each other.
Per-card windowed aggregates get sized by card count and by window length.
They're kept in the stream engine's own keyed state, and mirrored straight into the online store the request path reads from.
Past a certain point, that state simply stops fitting in memory alone.
Three fallback options exist on timeout here: approve, decline, or route to a slower path entirely.
Each one carries its own error cost — a false approve weighed against a false decline.
That choice gets decided and recorded as an ADR, never just defaulted to whichever branch happens to be easiest to code.
A timeout fallback is genuinely a business decision with a recorded cost, never just whichever branch happens to be easiest to implement.
The exact features and the exact decision live at scoring time get written straight to a log.
Weeks later, when a chargeback label finally arrives, that logged record — never today's feature values — is what actually trains the next model.
Logging the features and decision live at scoring time is genuinely what lets a label arriving weeks later train on what the model actually saw.

Notice what actually closed the gap between a comfortable average and a budget-blowing tail: building the budget at that steep percentile instead of the mean, treating the fallback as a priced decision instead of a default.
And logging what the model saw instead of trusting tomorrow's features to still match it.
The payment rate here grows a full tenfold.
The per-hop percentiles themselves barely move, but the feature-state size and the online store's own load both grow right along with it.
So what's actually the next bottleneck?
answer: Raising the timeout doesn't fix a hop that's genuinely slow — it just makes checkout wait longer before reaching that exact same fallback anyway.
The real next bottleneck here is the feature-state size and the load sitting on the store that actually holds it.
